title: Singly linked list: nodes & traversal
overview: A linked list stores each value in its own node, and each node points to the next one. This module builds nodes by hand (on the stack and with `new`), adds a constructor, links them with `next` pointers, and walks the list with a temporary pointer. It explains why linked lists exist when arrays are fixed-size and costly to insert into.

concepts.explain: A small class holding a value `val` and a pointer `next` to the following node. The last node's `next` is `NULL`, which marks the end.

Arrays have a fixed size and need shifting to insert in the middle. A linked list grows one node at a time and inserts by changing a couple of pointers. The cost: extra memory for each pointer and no O(1) access by index.
A constructor sets `val` and makes `next = NULL` as soon as the node is created, so you never forget to end the chain.
concepts.snippet: Node(int val) { this->val = val; this->next = NULL; }

concepts.explain: `p->val` is short for `(*p).val`: follow the pointer, then take the member. Chaining `head->next->next->val` walks two links.
`Node a(10);` lives on the stack and dies when the function ends. `new Node(10)` lives on the heap until deleted, so it can outlive the function that made it. Real lists use dynamic nodes.
The list is known only through `head`, the address of the first node. Lose it and you lose the whole list.
Copy `head` into `tmp` and move `tmp = tmp->next` until `tmp` is `NULL`. Stopping at `tmp->next == NULL` instead would skip the last node.
concepts.snippet: for(Node* tmp = head; tmp != NULL; tmp = tmp->next)

files.title: Creating and linking nodes by hand
files.what: Creates three stack nodes, sets their values, links them `a -> b -> c -> NULL`, and reads values through the links.
steps: Declare `Node a, b, c;` and set `val` to 10, 20, 30.
files.output_note: Three lines showing 10, 20, 30. The second and third values were reached through the pointers, not by naming `b` and `c`.
files.watch_out: Without a constructor, `val` and `next` start with garbage. Forgetting `c.next = NULL` would leave the list without a proper end.

files.title: Node with a constructor
files.what: Adds a constructor so `Node a(10)` sets the value and `next = NULL` in one step, then links and reads the nodes as before.
steps: The constructor `Node(int val)` uses `this->val = val` because the parameter has the same name as the member.
`Node a(10), b(20), c(30);` creates three ready nodes.

check.a: The parameter `val` hides the member `val`; `this->val` names the member explicitly.

files.title: Dynamic nodes with new
files.what: Creates nodes on the heap with `new` and links them through pointers.
steps: `Node* head = new Node(10);` makes a heap node and stores its address.
`(*head).next = a;` links head to a; no `&` is needed because `a` is already an address.
`a->next = b;` is the same thing written with the arrow.
files.watch_out: Heap nodes are never freed here. That is fine for a short demo, but long-running programs should `delete` nodes they no longer need.

check.q: Why is `head->next = a;` correct but `head->next = &a;` wrong here?
check.a: `a` is already a `Node*`; `&a` would be a `Node**`, the address of the pointer variable.

files.title: Printing a linked list
files.what: Walks a 4-node list with `tmp` and shows why the loop condition `tmp->next != NULL` misses the last node while `tmp != NULL` prints everything.
steps: Loop 1 runs while `tmp->next != NULL`: prints 10, 20, 30 and stops on node 40 without printing it.
Reset `tmp = head` and repeat: again 10, 20, 30, and `tmp` is left on node 40.
Loop 3 runs while `tmp != NULL`. It starts from node 40 (not from head), so it prints only 40.
files.output_note: `10 20 30` (loop 1), `10 20 30` (loop 2), then `40` (loop 3, starting where loop 2 stopped). Each value is on its own line.
files.watch_out: Loop 3 does not reset `tmp = head`, so it is not a full print. To print the whole list, reset `tmp` first and use `while (tmp != NULL)`.

check.q: What condition prints every node, including the last?

recap: A node = value + pointer to the next node; the last node points to NULL.
Use a constructor so `next` always starts as NULL.
Create list nodes with `new` so they outlive the function.
Traverse with a copy of head: `while (tmp != NULL) tmp = tmp->next;`.

check_yourself.q: Why does a linked list use more memory than an array for the same values?
check_yourself.a: Each node also stores a pointer (usually 8 bytes) alongside the value.

check_yourself.q: What is the cost of reaching the k-th element in a linked list, and why?
check_yourself.a: O(k): you must follow k links from the head; there is no direct indexing.

check_yourself.q: Name two array limitations that linked lists solve.
check_yourself.a: Fixed size decided up front, and slow insert/delete in the middle because elements must shift.
